Updated Nov 2026: this year the lecture came as a 20-page written handout (no slides). Part A (black) is the handout, kept in its wording and order. Part B (red) is every past-exam fact, grouped by complication. The Aldughaither summary (post-operative care & complications) is at the end.

Timings the handout repeats — atelectasis 24–48 h · pneumonia days 2–5 · reactionary haemorrhage < 24 h · SSI days 3–7 · anastomotic leak days 5–7 · dehiscence days 5–8 · PE days 7–10 (7–12 elsewhere in the handout) · secondary haemorrhage days 7–14 · MI immediate to day 3.

A1. The physiological stress response to surgery

  • The magnitude of the physiological response is directly proportional to the severity of surgical trauma. It is coordinated through activation of afferent nerve pathways and the innate immune system.

Neuroendocrine and inflammatory mediators

  • HPA axis & sympathetic nervous system: pain and tissue injury → CRF from the hypothalamus → ACTH from the pituitary → adrenal cortex secretes cortisol; sympathetic activation releases catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline) and glucagon.
  • Cytokine cascade: mononuclear cells at the injury site produce pro-inflammatory cytokines, primarily IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α → systemic inflammatory response, raised body temperature, stimulation of hepatic protein synthesis.
  • Immunological evolution: an initial pro-inflammatory state (SIRS) is rapidly counteracted by compensatory anti-inflammatory mechanisms (CARS), which, if prolonged, can lead to transient immunosuppression.

The "ebb and flow" model

Ebb phase (0–48 hours)Flow phase (days to weeks)
Driven byHypovolaemia, pain, intense sympathetic activityEvolves after resuscitation into a hypermetabolic, catabolic state
FeaturesReduced cardiac output, decreased basal metabolic rate, hypothermia, lactic acidosisHypermetabolism: resting energy expenditure ↑ 15–25% · skeletal-muscle catabolism (protein breakdown > synthesis) → amino acids diverted to vital viscera and wound repair → urinary nitrogen loss up to 14–20 g N/day (~500 g muscle/day in severe stress)
GoalVolume preservation and conservation of energy stores—
  • Hepatic acute-phase response: the liver reprioritizes synthesis toward positive acute-phase reactants (CRP, fibrinogen) while negative reactants (albumin) decline.
  • Post-operative insulin resistance & hyperglycaemia: cytokines and counter-regulatory hormones impair peripheral glucose uptake → transient diabetes-like hyperglycaemia.
  • Sodium and water retention: ADH and aldosterone promote renal fluid and sodium conservation → oliguria and expansion of extracellular fluid (oedema).

A2. Common early post-operative complications

  • Early complications typically arise within the first few hours to days after surgery.

A. Respiratory

  • Atelectasis: the single most common cause of early post-operative fever and dyspnoea, usually within the first 24–48 hours. Reduced FRC, shallow breathing from wound pain and mucus-plug retention → alveolar collapse.
  • Post-operative hypoxaemia: V/Q mismatch, respiratory depression from general anaesthetic or opioids, and atelectasis.
  • Pneumonia: secondary to persistent atelectasis or aspiration of gastric contents.

B. Cardiovascular & haemodynamic

  • Hypotension & hypovolaemia: unreplaced blood loss, third-space sequestration, or venous vasodilatation from epidural blockade or opioids.
  • Reactionary haemorrhage: delayed bleeding within 24 hours — dislodged clot or slipped ligature as blood pressure normalizes.
  • Cardiac events & arrhythmias: MINS (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery) or acute MI from surgical stress and O₂ supply/demand imbalance. Atrial fibrillation is the most frequent post-operative arrhythmia.
  • Post-operative shock: hypovolaemic (bleeding/fluid depletion), cardiogenic, or septic.

C. Renal & urinary

  • Post-operative urinary retention (POUR): common after pelvic, perineal, or spinal/epidural anaesthesia — altered detrusor neural control and over-distension.
  • Oliguria & AKI: oliguria < 0.5 mL/kg/h, most often prerenal (intra-operative hypovolaemia, hypotension, fluid loss).
  • UTIs: highly prevalent in catheterized patients.

D. Gastrointestinal

  • PONV: opioids, inhalational anaesthetics, delayed gastric emptying, surgical handling.
  • Paralytic (adynamic) ileus: transient impaired motility after abdominal manipulation, inflammation or opioids.
  • Anastomotic leak: typically days 5–7 — pyrexia, tachycardia, localized or generalized peritonitis, intra-abdominal collections.

E. Wound

  • Surgical site infection: superficial (skin/subcutaneous) or deep (fascia/muscle/organ space); typically days 3–7 with erythema, warmth, pain, purulent discharge.
  • Wound haematoma: blood under the incision — predisposes to infection; may need evacuation.
  • Wound dehiscence: partial or complete disruption of wound layers (often mid-laparotomy), usually days 5–8, frequently signalled by serosanguinous discharge.

F. Systemic & neurological

  • Post-operative pyrexia: a non-infectious physiological response in the first 24–48 hours; after day 3 it demands systematic evaluation for chest infection, UTI, wound infection, DVT or anastomotic leak.
  • Delirium/confusion: especially in the elderly — hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance, infection, pain, medication side effects.
  • VTE (DVT & PE): Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial damage); PE classically presents days 7–10.

A3. The deteriorating post-operative patient — reading the signs

  • Clinical deterioration often stems from systemic hypoperfusion or shock — tissue O₂ delivery (DO₂) fails to meet cellular requirements (VO₂). Because compensation preserves blood pressure and urine output until late, relying on vital signs alone can underdiagnose occult hypoperfusion.

Tachycardia

  • Typically the earliest compensatory response to a fall in stroke volume, circulating volume or SVR (baroreceptors, sympathetic tone, catecholamines).
  • Causes: hypovolaemia & haemorrhage · sepsis & SIRS (vasodilatation, hyperdynamic circulation) · inadequate analgesia · hypoxaemia (atelectasis, aspiration, PE) · cardiac events (fast AF, provoked by hypovolaemia, sepsis or electrolyte disturbance).
  • Caveats: patients on β-blockers or with pacemakers may not mount a tachycardia despite severe shock · the elderly have blunted responses, while fit young patients may keep a normal BP until rapid decompensation · prolonged tachycardia ↑ myocardial O₂ demand and ↓ diastolic filling → subendocardial ischaemia.

Metabolic acidosis

  • Hypoperfusion → anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → metabolic acidosis with a high base deficit.
  • Base deficit > 6 mmol/L strongly predicts severe shock, morbidity and mortality.
  • Severe acidosis depresses contractility, blunts the response to catecholamines and worsens clotting-factor dysfunction.
  • Part of the "lethal triad": acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy.
  • Respiratory compensation: tachypnoea and hyperventilation → compensatory respiratory alkalosis.

Elevated serum lactate

  • A quantitative marker of global tissue hypoxia, cellular dysoxia and oxygen debt.
  • Type A (hypoperfusion): hypovolaemic, cardiogenic or obstructive shock. Type B / septic: also from catecholamine-driven hyper-glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation ("cytopathic shock").
  • Lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L (or > 4) despite fluid resuscitation is a defining criterion of septic shock — mortality > 40%.
  • Occult hypoperfusion: normal BP and urine output but lactic acidosis persisting > 12 hours → 2–3× higher organ failure (MODS) and mortality.
  • Serial lactate clearance after fluid boluses = dynamic measure of resuscitation efficacy.

Systematic evaluation & resuscitation (handout flowchart)

StepAction
Post-operative deteriorationTachycardia, acidosis, high lactate
Airway & breathing (ABC)High-flow O₂ (SpO₂ > 94%), ABG/VBG
Screen & categoriseNEWS2 / qSOFA (RR, BP, mental status)
Circulatory resuscitationFluid challenge 250–500 mL crystalloid, evaluate the dynamic response
RespondersComplete resuscitation & target endpoints: normalise lactate and base deficit, ScvO₂ > 70%
Non- / transient respondersEscalate to ICU: central line & arterial monitoring · vasopressors/inotropes · identify & control the source (sepsis/bleed)
  • qSOFA: RR ≥ 22/min, altered mental status, systolic BP ≤ 100 mmHg.
  • Fluid challenge: 250–500 mL balanced crystalloid (e.g. Plasma-Lyte 148), or 30 mL/kg in septic shock, over 5–10 minutes.
ResponseMeaning
RespondersSustained normalization of HR, BP and urine output — volume depletion without ongoing loss
Transient respondersImprovement then recurrence of instability within 10–20 minutes — ongoing fluid loss or bleeding
Non-respondersMinimal response — profound hypovolaemia, active exsanguination, or cardiac/septic pump failure → invasive monitoring, vasopressors (noradrenaline) or inotropes (dobutamine)
  • Resuscitation endpoints: do not stop at a normal pulse and BP — the goal is lactate clearance (< 2 mmol/L), resolution of the base deficit, urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h, and ScvO₂ > 70%.

A4. Mechanisms of the major complications

Haemorrhage

TypeTimingCause
PrimaryIntra-operativeTissue injury, vascular division, incomplete haemostasis
ReactionaryFirst 24 hoursDislodged immature clots or slipped ligatures as BP normalizes and vasoconstriction relaxes after resuscitation
Secondary7–14 daysLocal infection eroding a vessel, pressure necrosis from drains, tissue sloughing
Non-surgical—Diffuse oozing from an acquired coagulopathy (dilution/consumption of clotting factors), not a discrete vessel
  • Haemorrhage → hypovolaemic shock → lethal triad spiral (lactic acidosis impairs clotting proteases; hypoperfusion and exposure cause hypothermia, worsening coagulopathy).

Hypovolaemia

  • Absolute loss: unreplaced blood loss, GI losses (vomiting, NG drainage, diarrhoea), excessive urine.
  • Relative loss (third-spacing): plasma-like fluid sequestered in interstitium, soft tissues or bowel lumen (inflammation, capillary leak, obstruction, ischaemia–reperfusion).
  • Peri-operative deprivation: pre-op fasting, evaporative loss from exposed viscera, inadequate replacement.
  • Presentation: ↓ stroke volume and cardiac output → tachycardia, cool, pale, clammy peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h).
  • Epidural blockade: loss of sympathetic tone → in a hypovolaemic patient, severe hypotension.

Sepsis & septic shock

  • A dysregulated host response to infection. Post-op sources: deep SSI, anastomotic leak (days 5–7), catheter-related bloodstream infection, UTI, pneumonia.
  • Cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) → endothelial activation, vasodilatation, ↑ capillary permeability.
  • Early / hyperdynamic phase: distributive shock — low SVR, high/normal cardiac output, warm well-perfused peripheries, bounding pulse, fever and rigors.
  • Late phase / cytopathic shock: fluid extravasation and myocardial depression → cool peripheries; lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L and acidosis from hypoperfusion plus mitochondrial dysfunction.

Pulmonary embolism

  • From DVT — Virchow's triad: stasis (immobility, muscle relaxants, long operations) · endothelial damage (pelvic, hip, lower-limb surgery) · hypercoagulability (malignancy, age, obesity, oestrogen, thrombophilia).
  • Classically late: days 7–12. The legs are frequently clinically normal when PE occurs.
  • Large PE obstructs RV outflow → obstructive shock: sudden dyspnoea, tachypnoea, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, hypoxia, right-heart strain, collapse or cyanosis.

Myocardial infarction & cardiac events

  • Stress, sympathetic surges, pain, hypovolaemia, hypercoagulability and tachycardia → supply/demand imbalance → Type II MI or MINS; plaque rupture (Type I) is less frequent post-op. Risks: advanced age, IHD, major abdominal/vascular surgery.
  • → Cardiogenic shock: low cardiac output, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, cold peripheries.
  • Often silent/atypical (residual anaesthesia, opioids mask pain) — presents as unexplained hypotension, sudden dyspnoea, confusion or new tachyarrhythmia (most commonly fast AF).

Respiratory

  • Atelectasis (24–48 h): anaesthetic agents ↓ FRC and impair mucociliary clearance; wound pain → shallow breathing and diaphragmatic splinting → resorptive collapse.
  • Pneumonia (days 2–5): persistent atelectasis, retained secretions, aspiration.
  • ARDS: sepsis, aspiration, ventilator volutrauma/barotrauma → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, loss of surfactant, stiff lungs, hypoxaemia refractory to O₂ (PaO₂:FiO₂ ≤ 40 kPa).
  • Pneumothorax: iatrogenic (central venous line insertion) or positive-pressure ventilation rupturing bullae.

Metabolic & electrolyte disturbances

  • Insulin resistance & hyperglycaemia (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, cortisol, adrenaline, glucagon) — ↑ infection and renal risk.
  • Refeeding syndrome: feeding a severely malnourished patient → insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells → severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia → arrhythmias, seizures, respiratory failure, death.
  • Fluid & electrolyte shifts: ADH/aldosterone retain water and sodium; TURP irrigation-fluid absorption → acute dilutional hyponatraemia (water intoxication); AKI → rapid hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis.
  • Lactic acidosis: marker of anaerobic metabolism (hypoperfusion or mitochondrial dysfunction).

A5. Assessing and managing the deteriorating patient

  • Rapid structured evaluation, concurrent resuscitation, early escalation, and timely surgical or radiological intervention.

Primary survey (ABCDE) — treat as you find

  • A — Airway — assess: Voice, patency, consciousness; obstruction from sedation/opioids, vomitus, or wound haematoma (thyroid/neck surgery). Manage: Chin lift/jaw thrust, suction, airway adjunct; GCS ≤ 8 → intubation; threatening neck haematoma → open the wound at the bedside.
  • B — Breathing — assess: RR (tachypnoea is often the earliest sign of deterioration), effort, expansion, breath sounds; SpO₂, ABG (PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH, base excess, lactate). Manage: High-flow O₂ (SpO₂ ≥ 95%); treat the cause: atelectasis (days 1–2) → analgesia + chest physiotherapy; pneumonia (days 2–5) → cultures + IV antibiotics; PE (days 7–12) → CTPA; pneumothorax/ARDS → CPAP/NIV or chest drain.
  • C — Circulation — assess: Pulse, BP, capillary refill, core–peripheral temperature gradient, hourly urine via catheter (> 0.5 mL/kg/h); 2 large-bore IVs; ECG, FBC, renal/liver function, coagulation, blood cultures, crossmatch. Manage: Classify shock: hypovolaemic (pale/cold) · septic/distributive (warm then cold, high lactate) · cardiogenic (↑ JVP, congestion, cold) · obstructive (tamponade, massive PE).
  • D — Disability — assess: GCS/AVPU, pupils, blood glucose. Manage: Exclude delirium from hypoxia, sepsis, hyponatraemia, drug toxicity/opioid overdose, hypoglycaemia.
  • E — Exposure — assess: Wounds (bleeding/dehiscence), drains (volume, colour: blood, pus, bile, enteric), distension, lower limbs for DVT. Manage: Protect dignity; active warming (forced-air blankets) to prevent the lethal triad.

Early warning scores & structured escalation

  • Track and trigger: a score such as NEWS2 (RR, SpO₂, BP, pulse, consciousness/new confusion, temperature) monitors trends and mandates escalation.
  • SBAR handover: Situation (current acute crisis) · Background (operation, post-op day, comorbidities, baseline) · Assessment (ABCDE findings, vitals, ABG — pH, base excess, lactate — and response to fluid) · Recommendation (senior review, critical-care bed, urgent CT, return to theatre).
  • Multidisciplinary escalation: senior surgeon, anaesthetist, critical care.

The Sepsis Six (within 1 hour)

#Action
1Senior clinician — immediate senior surgical/critical-care review
2Oxygen — high-flow, saturations > 94%
3Blood cultures — before antibiotics
4Antibiotics — empirical broad-spectrum IV covering likely surgical flora
5Fluids — crystalloid boluses (30 mL/kg in septic shock)
6Monitoring — serial lactate, base deficit, hourly urine output via catheter

Diagnostics & indications for re-exploration

Non-operative / imagingUrgent return to theatre
Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis — collections, anastomotic leak, bowel ischaemia (typically days 5–7)Reactionary/primary haemorrhage — active bleeding into drains/wound with hypovolaemic shock within 24 h
CTPA — suspected PEExpanding neck haematoma (thyroid/carotid) — open the wound immediately
Percutaneous drainage of local collectionsAnastomotic leak with peritonitis — relaparotomy, lavage, stoma, drainage
Dehiscence with evisceration — urgent resuturing in theatre
Acute compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch) — emergency fasciotomy
Damage-control surgery when the lethal triad is present (T < 34 °C, pH < 7.2 / lactate > 5 mmol/L, coagulopathy) — abbreviate surgery, laparostomy, ICU, planned secondary closure

A6. Teamwork, communication & "failure to rescue"

  • Errors and harm occur more often before or after an operation than during it. Failure to rescue = complications not recognized or managed in time to avert preventable death.
  • NEWS2 gives a common language across the team; SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) structures ward rounds; observation-chart trends (behaviour change, disorientation, rising RR) catch problems before decompensation.
  • Critical care outreach ("critical care without walls"): nurse-led teams bring ICU expertise to the wards — prevents unscheduled ICU admissions.
  • SBAR avoids "hinting and hoping" and bridges hierarchy gaps.
  • Operative notes: the surgeon documents clear post-op instructions — monitoring, expected recovery, and thresholds for calling back (e.g. drain output, blood loss). Recovery-to-ward handover = a safety check of airway, cardiovascular stability, pain and early wound/vascular complications.
  • Non-technical skills (NOTSS): shared mental models — pre-list briefing, the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out), debriefing; situation awareness and closed-loop communication; a culture where anyone can speak up.
  • M&M meetings: open, non-punitive peer review using the Swiss Cheese Model or London Protocol — look for latent conditions, not individual blame.

Part B — past-exam facts by complication. Everything below is from the gifts filed under this topic (midterm gifts + finals).

B1. Post-operative fever — timing

TimingUsual cause
Day 1–2 (48 h)Atelectasis (also malignant hyperthermia/transfusion reaction in the first hours)

Day 5–7Surgical site infection, intra-abdominal collection, leak

  • Fever 48 h after surgery → atelectasis. 441 ×12 442
  • POD 5: fever, dyspnea, chest pain, CXR consolidation, normal pulmonary vessels → hospital-acquired pneumonia. 438 Final
  • Best prevention of post-op pulmonary complications in a smoker → stop smoking 4–6 weeks before (6 weeks before lung surgery). 442 441 437
  • Severe COPD → pain control + incentive spirometry prevents post-op respiratory failure. 442
  • Heavy smoker agitated on POD 1 asking to smoke (nicotine withdrawal) → nicotine replacement patch. 442
  • SIRS on POD 2 (HR 110, RR 25, T 38.5, WBC 13k, normal BP) → SIRS; HR is a SIRS criterion; T 38.4 + WBC 14k support SIRS; the keyed ICU finding was a stress (gastroduodenal) ulcer. 442 432 ×3 441 441
  • Flushed, hypotensive and confused on POD 6 → septic shock (cultures, antibiotics, source). 430
  • Fever + hypotension + cold extremities, collapsed IVC, hyperdynamic LV → septic shock (↓ SVR / vasodilation). 442
  • Gram-negative bacteremia after shock + transfusion → translocation from the bowel. 432 ×2

  • SSI with pus → open the wound 441 442 434 ×4 431 ×2 430; mild erythema only → local care 437 437 ×2 439 439
  • Necrotizing fasciitis after lipoma excision/hernia repair → broad-spectrum antibiotics + urgent debridement. 442 442 ×2

  • The main difference: keloids extend beyond the original zone of injury. 429 Final ×2
  • Earlobe swelling 2 months after piercing in a dark-skinned woman → keloid 438 Final; a scar within the piercing 4 weeks later → hypertrophic scar (keyed). 437 Final
  • Keloid after median sternotomy → tell the patient to expect itching (keyed A; one version also wrote D, size fluctuation). 439 Final
  • Infected wound that is opened, irrigated and dressed → increased (prolonged) proliferative phase. Final
  • Huge infected necrotic sacral ulcer in a bed-bound diabetic → both the inflammatory and proliferative phases are increased (prolonged). 429 Final
  • Multivitamins in a well-nourished patient → no effect on healing. 437 Final ×2
  • Diabetes is the factor that significantly increases wound infection 430; tight glucose control reduces deep wound infection 438

B3. Intra-abdominal complications

  • Fever + RLQ pain after appendectomy for perforation, wound fine → intra-abdominal abscess; 6 cm collection → antibiotics + percutaneous drainage; 12 × 18 cm collection → percutaneous drainage. 439 441 434
  • Local peritonitis a few days after hemicolectomy (Crohn's) → anastomotic leak. 439
  • Fever and tachycardia after Billroth II → duodenal stump leak. 441 Final
  • Low-output enterocutaneous fistula (< 100 mL/day), normal distal bowel, no fever, POD 2 → continue enteral feeding + wound/skin care (most close spontaneously). 442 Final
  • Esophagectomy: drain output ~700 mL that turns milky white after oral intake → thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). 439 Final ×2
  • Post-sleeve: tachycardia + low urine output → leak 436; fever + hiccups → CT for leak/abscess 437; established leak → keyed surgical drainage, washout and repair 436 437 Final; septic shock after sleeve → leak 439 Final; gastric fistula → hypokalemia. 435 ×7
  • Paralytic ileus: distension, vomiting, sluggish sounds, air-fluid levels, normal vitals 4 days after laparotomy for perforated appendix. 437 ×2 436 ×2 438 Final ×6 Final
  • Post-op distension with air-fluid levels → NPO + nasogastric decompression. 439
  • Commonest long-term complication of appendectomy for perforation (12-year-old girl) → adhesive bowel obstruction. 432 Final ×2
  • Previous open appendectomy + obstruction → cause adhesions and bands 437 ×2; multiple scars, empty rectum → CT with oral + IV contrast 437; appendectomy 2 years ago + obstruction (X-ray) → keyed exploratory laparotomy. 438 ×2
  • Colicky central pain 4 years after Roux-en-Y, stable → keyed adhesions (internal hernia is the classic RYGB concern). 436
  • After bariatric surgery: ↑ gallstone formation (rapid weight loss). 429 ×2
  • Tense abdomen, oliguria, rising airway pressures, IAP 32 mmHg → abdominal compartment syndrome. 442
  • ICU patient (ventilated > 48 h, vasopressors) bleeding from NGT → prevent with acid suppression. 439
  • ERCP: commonest complication = pancreatitis 438 Final ×2; severe epigastric pain to the back + lipase > 3× normal 6 h after ERCP → post-ERCP pancreatitis. 442 Final
  • Fever and rash after splenectomy → OPSI (overwhelming post-splenectomy infection). 441 Final
  • Aorto-enteric fistula is not "always" after AAA surgery (usually secondary to AAA repair, but primary ones exist). 426

B4. Cardiopulmonary & vascular

  • Diabetic/hypertensive after laparoscopic hernia repair — monitor specifically for myocardial infarction in recovery (the key changed from airway to MI). 438 ×3 431 ×3
  • Chest pain, sweating and hypotension POD 1 → cardiogenic shock (MI). 430
  • HR 160, BP 90/60 after lung resection → atrial fibrillation. 439
  • Post-op chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension after APR (POD 5) → CT chest (CTPA) for PE. 438 ×10 437 Final ×2
  • Massive PE with BP responding to fluid → keyed LMWH. 430
  • Swollen painful calf → ultrasound (duplex) first 439; most common investigation for acute venous thrombosis → duplex. 427
  • First post-op day after lap chole → clinical assessment; on the ward → cardio-respiratory assessment. 430 ×2 434 ×2
  • Drowsy in recovery, SpO₂ 90%, normal pulse/BP → respiratory failure. 430
  • Collapse in recovery after appendectomy → bleeding (hypovolemic shock); a wound abscess is not a cause. 431 ×3 426
  • Excess opiates → high PaCO₂. 431 ×3

B5. Lines, catheters & procedures

  • Hypotension and desaturation 2 h after a subclavian line → tension pneumothorax 438 ×3; keyed most common complication of central-line insertion in the transfusion question → tension pneumothorax 437; least common → myocarditis 437; convulsion isn't a complication. 426
  • Septic ICU patient, 2 h after a right IJ line: restless, RR 30, rising O₂ and vasopressor needs → tension pneumothorax. 438 Final ×2
  • Local complication of angiography/angioplasty → pseudoaneurysm (systemic: contrast nephropathy, anaphylaxis). 438 Final
  • Infected PICC with S. aureus → remove the line, culture the tip, antibiotics. 439 ×9
  • Suprapubic catheter complications: infection, pelvic vessel injury, small-bowel injury — not liver injury. 437
  • Urinary retention after hernia repair despite 2 in-out catheterizations → Foley catheter with trial of void in a few days. 437 ×2
  • Unable to void 12 h after hernia repair, bladder up to the umbilicus → insert a Foley catheter. 435 Final ×2
  • After emergency hysterectomy: 800 mL/day clear fluid from the wound drain + 700 mL/day urine → ureteric injury (one kidney drains into the abdomen). 436 Final
  • Nerves at risk in inguinal hernia repair → ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, genitofemoral. 438 ×3
  • Post-dural-puncture headache after spinal/epidural: initial = bed rest, fluids, analgesics (caffeine); definitive (persistent > 24 h) = epidural blood patch. 436 438 435 436; headache 2 days after LP → best initial analgesia. 437 Final

B6. Endocrine & anesthetic

  • Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia (perioral tingling, cramps, Chvostek) → IV calcium gluconate. 442 441 439 434 ×5 431
  • Tingling and numbness after thyroidectomy → FIRST action: order a calcium level (keyed; then treat). 437 Final ×3
  • Commonest immediate complication of total thyroidectomy → hypocalcemia (parathyroid injury) 438 Final; lethargy and numb fingers/toes 2 weeks later → Chvostek's sign positive. 435 Final
  • Labs in post-thyroidectomy tetany (keyed) → low Ca, low PTH (option "low Ca, low phos, low PTH"; true hypoparathyroidism raises phosphate). 441 Final
  • After total thyroidectomy: hypoparathyroidism, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia — not hypercalcemia. 427
  • Hypothyroid patients risk myxedema coma after surgery. 438
  • Expanding neck hematoma with stridor after thyroidectomy → open the wound/evacuate at the bedside 442; old key: exploration. 427
  • Progressive swelling under the incision hours after thyroidectomy → wound exploration 438 Final ×2; stridor + swelling at the incision → hematoma 441 Final; most serious immediate complication in Graves' → neck hematoma. 429 Final
  • Malignant hyperthermia: prevent by avoiding succinylcholine + volatiles 442; treat with IV dantrolene. 442

B7. Blood, fluids & nutrition

  • DIC (bleeding from cannula sites, low platelets, high FDPs) → D-dimer. 438 ×7
  • Oozing after 6 units with prolonged PT/PTT → FFP. 441 ×2
  • Massive transfusion → hyperkalemia, citrate toxicity 431 ×2 431 ×3 426; transfusion transmits hepatitis B 426; acute hemolytic reaction (fever, chest/infusion-site pain, dark urine). 437 ×5 431 ×2
  • Dextran inhibits platelet aggregation. 429 ×2
  • TPN complication → hyperglycemia (also electrolyte disturbance, thrombosis, line sepsis) 438 ×8; persistent hyperglycemia on TPN → look for sepsis 438 ×4; TPN stopped abruptly → hypoglycemia. 438 ×3
  • NG suction → metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia 438 ×4 432 ×4; K⁺ 2.5 → IV KCl infusion 431 ×2; small-bowel fistula → metabolic acidosis. 439 432 ×3
  • Gentamicin with rising creatinine → stop gentamicin. 431 ×2

B8. Infections after surgery

Post-operative Care

  • Three phases of recovery from major surgeries:
  • Immediate: Post-anesthetic phase
  • Intermediate: after anesthesia recovery including period of hospitalization
  • Convalescent: transition from discharge to full recovery
Immediate post-operative phase:
  • The primary causes of death following surgery:
  • Acute pulmonary problems
  • Acute cardiovascular problems
  • Fluid derangements
  • Patient can be discharged from the recovery room once the cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurological status have returned to baseline (usually after 1-3 hours following surgery)
  • Post-operative orders:
  • Monitoring:
    • Vital signs:
    • Blood pressure, pulses, and respiration
    • Continuous ECG is indicated in PACU
    • Central venous pressure:
    • Indicated in operations with large fluid loss or fluid shifts
    • Invasive Swan-Ganz catheter or noninvasive measures may be used
    • Fluid balance:
    • Record administered fluids, blood loss, and urine output
    • A bladder catheter is inserted to monitor urine output
    • The surgeon should be notified if the patient didn’t produce urine after 6-8 hours post-surgery to assess for catheterization
    • Other types of monitoring:
    • ICP and level of consciousness after cranial surgery
    • Distal pulses after vascular surgery or cast patients
    • Expanding hematoma after thyroid surgery
    • “Post-operative check”:
    • Check the overall patient condition
  • Respiratory care:
    • Patient is supplemented with humidified O2 by mask or nasal prongs
    • Intubated patients require suctioning and monitoring to prevent aspiration
    • Deep breathing exercises via spirometer prevent atelectasis
  • Bed position and mobilization:
    • Patient should be turned from side to side every 30 minutes until conscious and then hourly for the first 8-12 hours to prevent atelectasis
    • Early ambulation is encouraged to reduce venous stasis; the upright position helps to increase diaphragmatic excursion
    • Support under the knees is given to reduce back pain, and head elevation at 30-45 degrees is done for certain conditions
  • Diet:
    • Patients at risk for emesis and pulmonary aspiration should have nothing by mouth (NPO) until some gastrointestinal function has returned, usually within 4 days
    • Patients with neurologic deficits may need evaluation by a speech and swallow team to determine their ability to tolerate liquids and solids of varying thicknesses.
  • Fluids and electrolytes:
    • Assessed based on maintenance needs, operative losses, and gastrointestinal loss from drains, fistulas, and stomas
  • Drainage tubes:
    • Assessed and examined daily to evaluate the character and quantity to avoid bleeding or fistulas
    • Should be labeled to avoid confusion and anchored properly
  • Medications:
    • Medication reconciliation is crucial to ensure patient safety
    • Antithyroid medication such as methimazole should not be routinely restarted after surgery for Graves' disease, and thyroid hormone supplementation may sometimes not be started until 4- 5 days afterward
    • Careful attention should be paid to the replacement of corticosteroids since postoperative adrenal insufficiency may be life-threatening, but over-supplementation can affect wound healing
    • Prophylaxis for postoperative nausea and vomiting can be useful
  • Labs and imaging:
    • Postoperative laboratory and radiographic examination should be used to detect specific abnormalities in high-risk groups
    • Chest radiographs are essential to confirm the proper placement of central venous lines and identify pneumothorax if not done in an operating room
  • Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS):
    • Protocols that are evidence-based and designed to standardize and streamline medical care
Intermediate post-operative phase:
  • Wound care:
  • The dressing removal and wound handling during the first 24 hours should be done with an aseptic technique
  • Dressings over closed wounds should be removed by the 3rd or 4th postoperative day
  • Dressings are removed earlier in the case of wet or contaminated wounds
  • Any drainage should be cultured for microorganisms
  • Vacuum dressings are replaced within 48-72 hours
  • Generally, skin sutures or staples may be removed by the 5th postoperative day and replaced by tapes
  • Sutures should be left in longer for incisions that cross skin crease (as in the groin or popliteal area), for incisions closed under tension, for some incisions in the extremities (hand, foot), and for incisions of any kind in debilitated patients
  • Patient may be allowed to shower or bathe by the 7th postoperative day (and often sooner, depending on the incision)
  • Drain management:
  • The external portion of the drain must be handled with an aseptic technique, and the drain must be removed as soon as it is no longer useful
  • Closed drains connected to suction devices (Jackson-Pratt or Blake drains) are preferable to open drains (such as Penrose) that predispose to wound contamination
  • Sump drains are useful when the amount of drainage is large or when drainage is likely to plug other kinds of drains. Some drains have extraluminal through which saline solution can be infused to aid in keeping the tube clear
  • Post-operative pulmonary care:
  • Reduced vital capacity, functional residual capacity (FRC), and pulmonary edema occur
  • Vital capacity decreases to about 40% of the preoperative level within 1-4 hours after major intra-abdominal surgery. It remains at this level for 12-14 hours, slowly increases to 60%-70% of the preoperative value by 7 days, and returns to the baseline level during the week after
  • FRC is near normal and is only decreased to 70% of the preoperative value, then gradually increases to normal levels at day 10
  • Such changes in FRC are larger in the elderly, obese, smokers, and patients with lung disease
  • Post-operative pulmonary edema is caused by high hydrostatic pressures (due to left-ventricular failure, fluid overload, decreased oncotic pressure), increased capillary permeability, or both
  • Signs and symptoms of pulmonary complications include fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, and altered mental status. Development of atrial fibrillation or an abnormal cardiac rhythm can often precede the identification of these pulmonary complications
  • Smokers are managed with nicotine patches or gum to avoid withdrawal symptoms
  • Many patients undergoing surgery are offered vaccination against pneumococcal or influenza infection during hospital stay
Respiratory Failure:
  • Early post-operative respiratory failure:
  • Within 48 hours post-surgery
  • Due to a mechanical problem and minimal changes to lung parenchyma
  • Seen in major operations (especially in chest), severe trauma, and preexisting lung disease
  • Usually develops within 1-2 hours without precipitating factors
  • Late post-operative respiratory failure:
  • After 48 hours post-surgery
  • Due to a trigger like PE and opioid overdose
  • Clinical features:
  • Tachypnea (> 25 breaths per minute)
  • Low tidal volume (< 4 ml/kg)
  • Labs:
  • PO2 < 60 mmHg
  • PCO2 > 45 mmHg
  • Treatment:
  • Endotracheal intubation and ventilatory support
  • Prevention:
  • Prevent atelectasis by breathing exercises
  • Avoid hypovolemia by giving fluids
  • In COPD, give epidural blocks or analgesics to relieve pain and thus prevent respiratory failure
Fluids and electrolytes:
  • Daily maintenance requirements for sensible and insensible loss in adults are about 1500-2500 mL, depending on the patient's age, gender, weight, and body surface area
  • A rough estimate can be obtained by multiplying the patient's weight in kg times 30
  • Maintenance requirement increases in fever and hyperventilation (increased catabolism rate)
  • No need to measure electrolyte levels in the case of short-period fluid requirement. However, it is indicated in:
  • Pre-existing electrolyte abnormalities
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Sepsis
  • Extra fluid loss
  • As a rule, 2000-2500 mL of 5% dextrose in normal saline or lactated Ringer solution is delivered daily
  • Potassium is not given in the first 24 hours because of increased levels post- surgery due to increased aldosterone and operative trauma
  • In most patients, fluid loss through a nasogastric tube is less than 500 ml/d and can be replaced by increasing the infusion used for maintenance by a similar amount. 20 meq of potassium should be added to every liter of fluid used to replace these losses
  • Postoperative ionized serum calcium in patients who have undergone thyroid or parathyroid surgery should be monitored and replaced
