Gastrointestinal tract:
  • Peristalsis is reduced after surgery but will return within:
  • Small intestine: 24 hours
  • Right colon: 48 hours
  • Left colon: 72 hours
  • Stomach and upper intestine: up to 3-4 days
  • Nasogastric tube insertion:
  • Goal: to protect against gastric distention and vomiting
  • Used in:
    • Esophageal and gastric resections
    • Marked ileus
    • Low level of consciousness
  • Once the nasogastric tube has been withdrawn, fasting is usually continued for another 24 hours, and the patient is then started on a liquid diet
  • Opioids interfere with gastric motility and should be avoided in the first post-operative week
  • Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy tubes:
  • Enteral nutrition started on the second day post-surgery regardless of the motility
  • Both tubes should not be removed before the third post-operative week
  • Hyperglycemia:
  • Diabetics should have their blood glucose monitored and recorded in admission
Transfusion:
  • Whole Blood:
  • 450-500 ml of donor blood
  • Contains red blood cells (Hct 35-45%), plasma, clotting factors, and anticoagulants
  • Indicated in massive blood loss with hypovolemia
  • Red blood cells:
  • 300-350 ml
  • RBCs from apheresis with (Hct 55-60%)
  • Indicated to increase O2 carrying capacity in anemic patients
    • Stable patients: threshold of 7 g/dl
    • Unstable patients with risk factors: higher than 7 g/dl
  • Every 1 unit of RBCs increases the hemoglobin by 1 g/dl and Hct by 3%
  • Patient donates RBCs 1 month before surgery
  • Washed red blood cells:
  • Washed with saline to remove 98% of proteins with Hct 75%
  • Indicated in anemic patients with severe allergic reactions and patients with IgA deficiency
  • Leukocyte-reduced red blood cells:
  • Removes 99.9% of contaminating leukocytes, leaving only 5 x 10^6 WBCs
  • Indicated for patients with recurrent Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR)
  • Reduces the risk of HLA and CMV-related reactions
  • Irradiated red blood cells:
  • RBCs irradiated with 25 Gy of gamma radiation
  • Indicated for patients who are at risk for associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD), such as:
    • Congenital severe immunodeficiency
    • Hematologic malignancy receiving intensive chemoradiotherapy
    • Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
    • Certain solid tumors (neuroblastoma and sarcoma)
    • Peripheral blood stem cell and marrow transplants
    • Recipients of fludarabine-based chemotherapy
    • Recipients of blood relatives or HLA-matched platelets
  • Frozen-deglycerolized red blood cells:
  • Removes 99.9% of contaminating plasma with Hct 75%
  • Indicated for patients with IgA deficiency
  • Platelets:
  • 250-300 ml with 3 x 10^11 platelets
  • Indicated for:
    • Active bleeding in thrombocytopenic patients
    • Nonthrombocytopenic patients with platelet dysfunction
    • Platelet count < 50,000/microliter in minor surgeries and line placements
    • Platelet count < 75-50,000/microliter in major surgeries
    • Neurosurgery, ophthalmic, and upper airway procedures should have at least 100,000/microliter
    • Not usually recommended in HIT, TTP, ITP, or Type 2B vWD
  • Fresh frozen plasma (FFP):
  • Contains albumin, clotting factors, and fibrinogen
  • Indicated for: Replacement of coagulation factors in patients with deficiencies of multiple clotting factors as occurs in:
    • The coagulopathy of liver disease
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
    • Warfarin overdose
    • Massive transfusions
  • After infusion of a 10-15 mL/kg dose, the activity of all coagulation factors increases by 20%-30%.
  • FFP should be used only if the INR is > 1.5 or the PT/aPTT is elevated more than 1.5 times the normal
  • FFP is the only replacement product for patients with rare disorders such as isolated factor deficiencies (V, X, XI) or C-1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
  • FFP is the first choice for fluid replacement in patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) undergoing therapeutic plasma exchange
  • Cryoprecipitate:
  • Cold-insoluble precipitate formed when FFP is thawed at 1-6°C, then resuspended in 10-15 mL of plasma (contains fibrinogen, factor 8, and vW factor)
  • Each unit of cryoprecipitate increases the fibrinogen level by 5-10 mg/dl
  • Indicated for:
    • Hypofibrinogenemia
    • Improvement of Platelet Aggregation and Adhesion in uremic patients to reduce bleeding
    • Factor XIII Deficiency
    • Not Recommended for Hemophilia A or vWD
  • Granulocyte Transfusions:
  • Made up of:
    • 1 x 10^10 or more granulocytes suspended in 200-300 mL plasma
    • About 1-3 x 10^11 platelets
    • 10-30 mL RBCs
  • Indicated for:
    • Severely neutropenic patients (ANC < 0.5 x 10^9/L) with bacterial sepsis not responding to antibiotics in 48-72 hours
  • Post-operative pain:
  • Communication: It is important to understand patient needs
  • Parenteral opioids: mainstay treatment for post-operative pain
    • Morphine:
    • Most widely used
    • Given intravenously, either intermittently or continuously, and requires continuous monitoring
    • Side effects: respiratory depression, nausea, vomiting, and clouded sensorium
    • Meperidine:
    • 1/8th the potency of morphine
    • Shorter duration than morphine
    • Similar effects and side effects
    • Requires continuous monitoring when given IV
    • Others:
    • Hydromorphone: 1-2 mg IM every 2-3 hours
    • Methadone:
    • 10 mg IM every 10 hours
    • Long half-life (6-10 hours)
    • Used to treat morphine withdrawal symptoms
  • Parenteral non-opioids:
    • Ketorolac:
    • 30 mg has the same efficacy as 10 mg morphine
    • Advantage: No respiratory depression
    • Complications: (not reported in short-term use)
    • GI ulceration
    • Impaired renal function
    • Impaired coagulation
  • Oral Analgesics:
    • Aspirin is avoided because of bleeding risks but is used to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in certain patients
    • Usually, a combination of acetaminophen and codeine is enough
  • Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA):
    • Allows patients to manage their pain relief by controlling the frequency of analgesic administration within safe limits
  • Continuous epidural analgesia:
    • Requires a similar dosage, has a slightly delayed onset of action, provides substantially longer pain relief, and is associated with better preservation of pulmonary function
    • Given as 0.2-0.8 mg/h, with or without the addition of 0.25% bupivacaine
    • Advantages: Patients are alert and have better GI function
    • Disadvantages: Pruritus, urinary retention, and nausea
    • Also, respiratory depression may occur
  • Intercostal block:
    • May be used to decrease pain following thoracic and abdominal operations
    • Doesn’t relieve pain completely as it doesn’t reach the visceral afferent nerves but does relieve muscle spasms
    • Advantage: No hypotension as in epidural and produces analgesia for 3-12 hours
    • Disadvantage:
    • Pneumothorax with insertion
    • Reduced by placing a catheter in the pleura or intercostal space
  • Special considerations:
  • Cognitive modalities and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may be considered in chronic pain patients or patients with expected long-term symptomatology
Convalescent phase:
  • All the necessary arrangements should be made to ensure proper discharge

Post-operative Complications

Wound complications:
  • Seroma:
  • Localized fluid collection with no pus or blood
  • Made up of serous fluid that collects and delays wound healing and predisposes to infections
  • They either resorb or require needle aspiration for evacuation
  • In vascular-related seromas, it may be best to avoid aspiration as this may injure the underlying blood vessels
  • Hematoma:
  • Collection of blood and clot near surgical incision
  • Presents as elevated discoloration around wound edges causing swelling and discomfort
  • Coagulopathy (liver disease) and anticoagulants increase its risk
  • Small hematomas often resolve, but larger ones may require intervention
  • Hematomas of the neck (thyroid, parathyroid, carotids) are dangerous due to their compression around adjacent structures and require evacuation, ligation of blood vessels, and wound reclosure
  • Surgical site infections (SSIs):
  • Infection where the surgery was performed
  • Classified into:
    • Superficial incisional: limited to skin/subcutaneous tissue
    • Deep incisional: involves muscle/fascia
    • Organ space
  • Risk factors:
    • Patient factors:
    • Age (neonates and >65)
    • Nutritional status
    • Diabetes
    • Smoking
    • Obesity
    • Coexistent infection at another site
    • Microorganism colonization
    • Altered immune response
    • Duration of postoperative stay
    • Operative factors:
    • Preoperative antiseptic preparation
    • Antimicrobial prophylaxis
    • Use of foreign materials
    • surgical site and technique
  • Prevention:
    • Use of antiseptic technique
    • Meticulous surgical techniques
    • Pre-operative antibiotic administration
    • Antibiotics:
    • Clean cases (e.g., inguinal hernia repair) require coverage for skin flora (cefazolin)
    • Clean-contaminated cases (e.g., gastrointestinal surgeries) need Gram-negative and anaerobic coverage (cefazolin + metronidazole for colectomy)
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical symptoms: Localized pain, warmth, erythema, and purulent drainage
    • Deep or organ-space SSIs: May require imaging or wound exploration
    • Complications: Can lead to wound dehiscence or anastomotic breakdown
  • Treatment:
    • Superficial infections: Managed at bedside with incision opening, irrigation, and debridement, followed by regular wound care
    • Deep incisional & organ-space infections: Often require reoperation for exploration, drainage, and debridement.
    • Implanted materials involvement: Infected implants (e.g., mesh) must be removed
    • Alternative approach: Percutaneous drainage under image guidance if surgery poses high risks
    • Antibiotics: Supportive but do not eliminate the infection without addressing the primary source
  • Classification of surgical wounds:
  • Rare in the first few days post-surgery, except necrotizing soft tissue within the first 24 hours caused by S. pyogenes or C. perfringens
  • Presents as:
    • Pain with mobilization
    • Crepitus
    • Bullae/Blisters
    • SIRS
    • Sepsis
  • Wound dehiscence:
  • Partial or complete disruption of any or all layers of an operative wound
  • Evisceration: Rupture of all abdominal wall layers with protrusion of abdominal viscera (rare but a surgical emergency) Risk Factors:
    • Systemic factors: Diabetes, uremia, impaired immune function, steroid use, jaundice, sepsis, malnutrition, cancer, obesity, smoking
    • Local factors: Inadequate closure, intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining, or vomiting), Deficient wound healing (foreign materials), or peri-incisional fluid collections.
    • Type of incision (e.g., transverse, midline) does not influence dehiscence risk
  • Prevention:
    • Proper wound closure
    • Retention sutures: Used in high-risk patients to reduce evisceration risk (they do not prevent dehiscence).
    • Managing intra-abdominal pressure: Encourage coughing with a pillow, use abdominal binders, administer stool softeners.
  • Presentation & Diagnosis
    • Timing: Most common between postoperative days 5–8 (when tissue strength is weakest)
    • Early signs: Drainage from the incision
    • Severe cases: Sudden wound separation with a "popping" sensation, often after coughing or retching
  • Management
    • Fascial dehiscence without evisceration: Managed electively with prompt reclosure.
    • Stable partial wound disruption: If the patient is a poor surgical candidate, treatment may be delayed, but an incisional hernia is expected
    • Infected wounds: Delayed closure until infection resolves (typically 6–7 months), with antibiotics covering previously isolated organisms at the time of hernia repair
    • Evisceration: Requires immediate surgical intervention
  • Anastomotic Leak:
  • Type of wound dehiscence occurring due to disrupted healing between visceral anastomoses and triples the mortality rates
  • Occur in 1–24% of anastomoses, with higher rates in low pelvic anastomoses compared to more proximal ones
  • Risk Factors:
    • Systemic factors: Age, malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies, steroid use, obesity, diabetes, smoking, inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis), previous radiation/chemotherapy, anemia
    • Local factors: Tension at the anastomosis, poor blood flow, hypotension, radiation exposure, contamination
  • Avoid tension at the suture line to ensure adequate blood flow
  • Most common between postoperative days 5–7 (first 24 hours if due to technical issues like suture-related)
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical signs: Tachycardia (first sign), Pain, fever, peritonitis, and purulent or fecal drainage from the wound
    • Radiographic findings: Gas or fluid collections near the anastomosis, contrast leakage seen on oral contrast/enema studies
    • Intraoperative findings: Contamination with gastrointestinal contents, visible anastomotic disruption
  • Management:
    • Nonoperative approach (mild cases): Observation, bowel rest, antibiotics, percutaneous drainage of abscesses
    • Operative intervention (common in severe cases): Wide drainage, proximal diversion, and/or anastomotic revision
Neurological complications:
  • Cerebrovascular Accidents (CVA):
  • Most common cause: Thromboembolic events within 72 hours postoperatively
  • Less common causes: Air embolism, fat embolism, paradoxical embolism, cervical arterial dissection, hemorrhagic stroke, lacunar ischemic stroke, and spinal cord infarctions
  • Risk Factors
    • Patient-related: History of stroke, atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, COPD, renal disease, advanced age, cancer, smoking
    • Surgical & intraoperative:
    • Hypotension
    • Cessation of anticoagulation increases stroke risk, especially in patients with mechanical heart valves, atrial fibrillation with prior stroke, hypercoagulability, and recent deep vein thrombosis (≤30 days)
  • Stroke Risk by Surgery Type
    • Highest risk (10%) – Multivalve replacement surgeries
    • Moderate risk (≤6%) – Carotid endarterectomy or stenting (varies based on symptoms, plaque anatomy, and stenosis degree)
    • Low risk (<1%) – Hemicolectomy.
    • Cardiac surgery: Extracorporeal circulatory pumps increases risk due to micro emboli bypassing the lungs
    • Carotid surgery: Stroke risk depends on symptomatology, plaque characteristics, and ischemic duration from clamping
  • Diagnosis
    • Symptoms: Acute neurological deficits
    • Imaging: Non-contrast CT of the head to differentiate ischemic vs. hemorrhagic stroke
  • Additional tests:
    • ECG – Check for acute cardiac events/arrhythmias
    • Echocardiogram – Evaluate for cardiac embolism or patent foramen ovale
    • Carotid ultrasound – Detect atherosclerotic plaque buildup
  • Management
    • Ischemic Stroke:
    • Aspirin & statins should be started
    • Thrombolysis (tPA) may be given if within 4.5 hours of stroke onset and no major bleeding risk
    • Permissive hypertension strategy: Maintain BP < 185/110 mmHg in the acute phase
    • Hemorrhagic Stroke:
    • Stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets and administer reversal agents
    • Aggressive blood pressure control (target systolic BP < 150 mmHg)
    • Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring and neurosurgical intervention for hematoma decompression if mass effect is present
  • Paraplegia:
  • Rare but devastating complication that results from reduced blood flow to the spinal cord
  • High-Risk Patients:
    • Procedures involving the descending thoracic aorta (both open and endovascular) may affect the artery of Adamkiewicz
    • Patients with vascular disease, spinal stenosis, or intraoperative hypotension (risk increases with epidural placement)
    • History of aortic aneurysms, especially when combined with perioperative hypotension
  • Determinants of Spinal Cord Injury Severity:
    • Ischemic duration and severity of ischemia
    • Success in reestablishing blood supply
    • Extent of reperfusion injury
  • Prevention:
    • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage to reduce spinal cord pressure
    • Hypothermia to minimize metabolic demand
    • Partial bypass of blood flow during aortic procedures
    • Maintaining adequate blood pressure (normotension) to ensure spinal perfusion
  • Sexual Dysfunction:
  • Typically seen in:
    • Deep pelvic surgeries (e.g., prostatectomy, hysterectomy, rectal cancer resection)
    • Surgeries affecting blood flow (e.g., cardiac surgery, aortic reconstruction)
  • Pathogenesis
    • Nerve damage: Injury to nerves essential for sexual function, particularly the sacral plexus (e.g., after abdominoperineal resection)
  • Management & Patient Counseling
    • Preoperative discussion: Patients should be informed about potential sexual dysfunction before surgery
    • Psychogenic causes: Often resolved with reassurance
    • Persistent impotence (beyond 4–6 weeks): Requires specialist consultation
Psychiatric complications:
  • Post-operative Delerium:
  • Waxing and waning disturbance in consciousness with symptoms ranging from hypoactive to hyperactive states and possible psychosis.
  • Risk Factors
    • Predisposing factors (patient-related)
    • Reduced cognitive reserve (e.g., dementia, depression, advanced age).
    • Reduced physical reserve, sensory impairment, malnutrition, dehydration, and substance abuse.
    • Precipitating factors (surgery-related):
    • Use or withdrawal of certain medications (anesthetics, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants, antihistamines).
    • Pain, hypoxemia, electrolyte imbalances, sleep-wake disturbances, environmental change (e.g., ICU stay).
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Hyperactive delirium: Restlessness, agitation, hallucinations, delusions.
    • Hypoactive delirium: Reduced movement, minimal communication, unresponsiveness (often mistaken for depression, anxiety, or calmness and thus underdiagnosed).
    • Patients may fluctuate between them.
  • Prevention
    • Frequent orientation (reminding the patient of time, place, and reason for hospitalization).
    • Early mobilization after surgery and exclude sepsis.
    • Consistent use of home sensory devices (e.g., glasses, hearing aids) in the hospital.
    • Careful titration of sedatives in ICU (preferred agent: dexmedetomidine, as it has a lower risk of delirium).
  • Management
    • Early psychiatric consultation
    • Identify and treat underlying causes
    • Typical & atypical antipsychotics for symptom control
    • Preoperative counseling can reduce postoperative emotional disturbances
  • Alcohol Withdrawal:
  • Alcohol dependence includes tolerance, compulsive use, and withdrawal symptoms
  • Symptoms typically start 6–24 hours after the last drink and peak within 24–48 hours.
  • Symptoms & Progression
    • Early symptoms (6–24 hours): Tremors, sweating, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, agitation.
    • Seizures (12–48 hours): May occur in some patients.
    • Delirium Tremens (DTs) (48–96 hours):
    • Most severe and life-threatening
    • Symptoms: Auditory/visual hallucinations, confusion, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis), dehydration.
    • Untreated DTs can lead to cardiovascular or respiratory collapse and death
  • Prophylaxis & Treatment
    • First-line prophylaxis & treatment: Benzodiazepines.
    • Alternatives: Chlormethiazole or direct alcohol administration.
    • Monitoring
    • Supportive care:
    • Vitamin B1 (thiamine) & magnesium sulfate to prevent complications
    • Restore nutrition, correct electrolyte imbalances, and ensure hydration.
    • Frequent vital sign assessment.
    • Limit physical restraints unless necessary for violent behavior.
    • With proper care, most patients recover within 72 hours.
  • Pain:
  • Pain is common postoperatively, and opioid use poses significant risks.
  • Risk factors for chronic opioid use:
    • Male gender, age > 50 years, history of substance abuse, depression.
    • Surgery itself is an independent risk factor.
  • Complications
    • Short-term risks: Oversedation, respiratory suppression, delirium, ileus.
    • Long-term risks:
    • Tolerance, dependence, immunosuppression.
    • Opioid-induced endocrinopathy (e.g., sexual dysfunction, depression, fatigue).
    • Increased inpatient mortality.
  • Multimodal Analgesia (Alternative Pain Management)
    • Goal: Reduce opioid use by incorporating non-opioid analgesia.
    • Key pain management strategies:
    • Scheduled acetaminophen & NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for baseline pain control.
    • Limited opioid use
Cardiac complications:
  • Generally, oral anticoagulants should be stopped 3-5 days before surgery
  • Patient at high risk of thromboembolic disease should receive heparin until 6 hours before the operation. Then, it is restarted 36-48 hours after surgery
  • Beta-blockers are used only when the patient regularly uses them
  • Peri-operative Myocardial Infarction:
  • Occurs in 0.4% of all surgical patients and 5–12% in patients with atherosclerotic disease (e.g., carotid endarterectomy, peripheral vascular grafts). Key risk factors:
    • Preoperative congestive heart failure.
    • Ischemia detected on cardiac stress tests.
    • Advanced age (>70 years).
    • Consider coronary revascularization before major elective surgery in patients with angina.
  • Triggers & Clinical Presentation
    • Precipitating factors: Hypotension, hypoxemia.
    • Symptoms:
    • Typical: Chest pain, hypotension, cardiac dysrhythmias.
    • Atypical: Asymptomatic due to anesthesia or postoperative analgesia.
  • Diagnosis
    • Electrocardiographic changes.
    • Elevated cardiac enzymes (troponin-I).
  • Prevention
  • Delay elective surgery for up to 6 months after an MI.
  • Optimize congestive heart failure and hypertension before surgery.
  • Management
    • ICU monitoring
    • Anticoagulation (if feasible)
    • Definitive treatment:
    • PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) for stent placement if within 120 minutes of diagnosis.
    • Fibrinolysis if within 12 hours but PCI is unavailable.
    • CABG (coronary artery bypass graft) only if PCI/fibrinolysis fails or there are mechanical complications (e.g., ventricular rupture, acute valvular dysfunction).
    • Post-treatment:
    • Dual antiplatelet therapy (for stent placement).
    • Lifelong statin therapy.
  • Post-operative Cardiac Failure:
  • Most common cause: Fluid overload with limited myocardial reserve
  • Other causes:
    • Postoperative myocardial infarction.
    • Dysrhythmias with high ventricular rates.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Progressive dyspnea, hypoxemia.
    • Chest X-ray findings: Diffuse pulmonary edema.
    • Diagnostic clues:
    • Decreased PaO2.
    • Abnormal chest X-ray.
    • Elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure.
  • Management
    • Pulmonary artery line placement to monitor filling pressures.
    • Immediate preload & afterload reduction:
    • Preload reduction: Diuretics ± nitroglycerin.
    • Afterload reduction: Sodium nitroprusside.
  • Long-term mortality reduction: ACE inhibitors & beta-blockers.
  • Supportive care and respiratory support:
    • Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV)
    • (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) (PEEP)
  • Dysrhythmias:
  • General anesthesia depresses the myocardium and may sensitize it to catecholamines, increasing dysrhythmia risk.
  • High-risk cardiac patients may benefit from regional anesthesia (for procedures below the umbilicus).
  • Most dysrhythmias occur intraoperatively or within the first 3 postoperative days, especially after thoracic procedures.
  • Triggers:
  • Anesthetic agents (e.g., halothane, cyclopropane).
  • Sympathomimetic drugs.
  • Induction-associated hypercapnia.
  • Postoperative dysrhythmias are often due to reversible factors:
  • Electrolyte imbalances, hypoxemia, stress during anesthesia emergence.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Most patients are asymptomatic.
    • Some may experience chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea.
  • Types of Dysrhythmias & Management
    • Supraventricular Dysrhythmias (e.g., Atrial Fibrillation, Atrial Flutter with RVR)
    • Decreases cardiac output & coronary blood flow may cause hypotension & hypoperfusion.
    • Management:
    • Hemodynamically unstable: Immediate cardioversion.
    • Stable: Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or digoxin.
    • Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs)
    • Triggered by: Hypercapnia, hypoxemia, pain, fluid overload.
    • Treatment: Oxygen, sedation, analgesia, correction of fluid/electrolyte imbalances.
    • Ventricular Dysrhythmias (Ventricular Tachycardia [VT] & Ventricular Fibrillation [VF])
    • High risk of sudden cardiac death.
  • Supraventricular Tachycardia
    • Management:
    • Hemodynamically unstable VT: Synchronized cardioversion.
    • Stable VT: Adenosine (first-line), followed by lidocaine, procainamide, amiodarone, or sotalol if needed.
    • Ventricular Fibrillation & Pulseless VT: Defibrillation & chest compressions (ACLS protocol).
  • Heart Block:
  • Types & Severity
    • First-degree & second-degree heart block – Usually well tolerated.
    • Third-degree (complete) heart block – Indicates serious underlying disease and requires a pacemaker.
  • Risks & Consequences
    • Patients with heart block are at risk of symptomatic bradycardia, leading to hypoperfusion and poor cardiac output.
    • Severe bradycardia can have serious consequences, including syncope, heart failure, or sudden cardiac arrest.
  • Management
    • First- & second-degree heart block: Usually does not require intervention unless symptomatic.
    • Third-degree heart block: Requires pacemaker implantation for proper cardiac function.
Pulmonary complications:
  • Most common single cause of morbidity post-surgery and second most common cause of death post-surgery in > 60-year-old patients
  • Post-operative respiratory failure:
  • Ventilation > 48 hours or reintubation.
  • Severity spectrum:
    • Acute Lung Injury (ALI): P/F ratio 200–300.
    • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): P/F ratio < 200.
  • Risk Factors
    • Preoperative: Poor lung function, age, comorbidities (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, cardiovascular disease), smoking.
    • Intraoperative: Lung injury, prolonged surgery, gas anesthesia, fluid overload, blood transfusions.
    • Postoperative: Aspiration, inadequate pain control, poor ventilation, infections.
  • Prevention
    • Preoperative: Respiratory training, medication optimization, smoking cessation, functional status assessment.
    • Intraoperative: Minimize surgery duration, optimize volume management, and avoid unnecessary transfusions.
    • Postoperative:
    • Fast-track extubation.
    • Effective pain management.
    • Breathing exercises & physiotherapy.
    • Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) & bronchodilators.
    • Thrombosis prophylaxis & antibiotics if indicated.
  • Treatment
    • Early tracheostomy
    • Protective ventilation:
    • Tidal volume: 6 mL/kg body weight.
    • Peak pressure: <30 mm Hg.
    • PEEP goal: 10–20 mm H₂O.
    • Early mobilization & bronchoscopy if needed.
    • Severe cases: (ECMO).
    • Avoid excessive fluids to prevent pulmonary edema.
  • Pulmonary Embolism:
  • Pulmonary arterial obstruction.
  • Incidence: 0.3%–30% after surgery.
  • Mortality rate: 16%–31%.
  • Causes:
    • Thrombus (most common).
    • Tumor, air, fat, amniotic fluid embolism.
  • Clinical Features
    • Complications: Pulmonary infarction, impaired gas exchange, cardiovascular compromise.
    • Common symptom: Sinus tachycardia.
    • Other symptoms: Pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, tachypnea, hypoxia, respiratory alkalosis.
    • Severe cases: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance → right ventricular failure → decreased left-ventricular preload →
    • reduced stroke volume & cardiac output → cardiopulmonary
    • collapse.
  • Diagnosis
    • Hemodynamically stable patients:
    • First-line: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) – Detects filling defects.
    • Alternative (if contrast allergy or renal impairment): Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan.
    • If neither is available: Echocardiogram to assess right- ventricular function.
    • If workup is inconclusive but clinical suspicion is high, empiric anticoagulation should be started.
  • Management
    • Stable patients: Oxygen & anticoagulation (e.g., heparin, direct oral anticoagulants).
    • If anticoagulation is contraindicated: Inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placement.
    • Unstable patients (SBP <90 mmHg for >15 min or requiring vasopressors):
    • Systemic thrombolysis or suction embolectomy.
  • Origins of Pulmonary Emboli
    • Most common: Thromboemboli from proximal deep veins (iliac, femoral, popliteal).
    • Risk factors (Virchow’s triad):
    • Venous stasis (e.g., prolonged immobilization, surgery, trauma).
    • Endothelial injury (e.g., vascular trauma).
    • Hypercoagulable state (e.g., cancer, hormone therapy, obesity, smoking).
  • Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES)
    • Occurs in 90% of patients with long bone fractures or joint replacements but rarely causes symptoms.
    • Can also occur from blood transfusions, IV fat emulsions, or bone marrow transplantation.
    • Symptoms:
    • Neurologic dysfunction, respiratory insufficiency, petechiae (axillae, chest, proximal arms).
    • Lab findings: ↓ Hematocrit, thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities.
    • Diagnosis: Clinical findings (no definitive test).
    • Treatment: Supportive care until symptoms resolve.
  • Atelectasis:
  • Most common pulmonary complication after surgery.
  • Higher risk in: Smokers, elderly, obese, and patients with underlying respiratory disease.
  • Occurs most frequently in the first 48 hours postoperatively.
  • Causes
    • Obstructive causes: Mucous plugs, blood clots, sedation, endotracheal tube malposition.
    • Nonobstructive causes:
    • Bronchiolar closure in lung-dependent areas due to reduced lung volume (common in smokers & elderly).
    • Poor respiratory effort → Shallow breathing & failure to hyperinflate the lungs → Reduced alveolar size & volume.
    • Loss of surfactant (e.g., pneumonia).
  • Symptoms & Diagnosis
    • Fever, tachypnea, tachycardia.
    • Physical exam findings:
    • Diaphragm elevation.
    • Scattered rales and decreased breath sounds.
  • Prevention
    • Early mobilization, frequent position changes.
    • Encourage coughing & use of an incentive spirometer.
    • Preoperative respiratory exercises.
  • Treatment
    • Airway clearance techniques:
    • Chest percussion, coughing, deep suctioning.
    • Nebulized bronchodilators & mucolytics
    • Obstructive atelectasis may require intrabronchial suctioning via endoscope
  • Pulmonary Aspiration:
  • Key reflexes:
    • Laryngeal adductor reflex (vocal cord closure).
    • Esophagoglottal closure reflex.
    • Pharyngoglottal closure reflex.
  • Compromised protection occurs with:
    • Depressed mental status.
    • Foreign bodies (e.g., nasogastric or endotracheal tubes).
  • Severity Factors
    • Extent of pulmonary injury depends on:
    • Volume aspirated.
    • pH of the aspirate (pH ≤ 2.5 causes immediate chemical pneumonitis → local edema, inflammation, secondary infection risk).
    • Frequency of aspiration events.
    • Aspiration of solids: Can cause airway obstruction → Pulmonary abscess formation.
    • Commonly affected lung regions: Basal segments (right side more than left due to anatomy).
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Early symptoms (within hours): Tachypnea, rales, hypoxemia.
    • Less frequent symptoms: Cyanosis, wheezing, apnea.
  • Prevention
    • Preoperative:
    • Fasting before surgery.
    • Proper patient positioning.
    • Careful intubation technique.
    • Pre-induction H₂-blockers or proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) for high-risk patients.
  • Management
    • Restore airway patency & prevent further lung damage.
    • Immediate treatment:
    • Endotracheal suctioning (diagnostic & therapeutic).
    • Endotracheal bronchoscopy (for solid material removal if needed).
    • Fluid resuscitation to address hypovolemia.
    • Early initiation of antibiotics to prevent secondary infection.
  • Post-operative pleural effusion and pneumothorax:
Postoperative Pleural Effusion
  • Higher risk in patients with:
    • Free peritoneal fluid at the time of surgery.
    • Postoperative atelectasis.
  • Causes & Implications
    • Early postoperative effusions – Usually benign, no intervention needed.
    • Late postoperative effusions in patients without cardiac or pulmonary disease may suggest subdiaphragmatic inflammation (e.g., subphrenic abscess, acute pancreatitis).
  • Management
    • No intervention is recommended if the effusion does not compromise respiratory function.
    • If infection is suspected, obtain a sample via needle aspiration.
    • Symptomatic effusions require thoracostomy tube placement, which can be removed once the accumulation slows.
Postoperative Pneumothorax
  • Causes & Risk Factors
    • Central venous line (CVL) placement.
    • Positive-pressure ventilation in patients with underlying lung disease.
    • Iatrogenic pleural injury during paraesophageal hernia repair, nephrectomy, or adrenalectomy.
  • Management
    • Small-caliber thoracostomy tube
Gastrointestinal complications:
  • Functional obstruction (Ileus):
  • Occur due to decreased gut propulsive activity caused by anesthesia and surgical manipulation.
  • Causes & Risk Factors
    • Medications (e.g., opioids).
    • Electrolyte abnormalities.
    • Inflammatory conditions (e.g., pancreatitis, peritonitis).
    • Pain and the degree of operative manipulation.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Symptoms: Nausea, bloating, burping, hiccups.
    • Signs: Abdominal distension, tympany on exam.
    • Imaging: Dilated bowel loops on abdominal X-ray.
  • Timeline of Return to Normal Peristalsis
    • Non-abdominal surgery: Within 24 hours.
    • Minimally invasive surgery: Faster recovery than open procedures.
    • Laparotomy recovery:
    • Gastric peristalsis returns in about 48 hours post-op.
    • Colonic activity returns after 48 hours, starting at the cecum and progressing caudally.
    • Small bowel function returns after colonic function.
  • Management
    • Supportive care (no definitive therapy available).
    • Therapeutic nasogastric (NG) tube for patients with significant nausea & vomiting.
    • Return of peristalsis noted by: Mild cramps, passage of flatus, return of appetite.
    • Early feeding is encouraged (e.g., ERAS protocols promote feeding as early as postoperative day 0).
  • Mechanical obstruction:
  • Most common cause: Postoperative adhesions.
  • Other causes: Internal (mesenteric) hernia.
  • Clinical Course & Symptoms
    • Short period of normal bowel function before symptoms appear.
    • Symptoms resemble paralytic ileus, making diagnosis difficult.
    • Signs: Abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, absent or high- pitched bowel sounds.
  • Diagnosis
    • Abdominal plain film (X-ray): Air-fluid levels in small bowel loops suggest mechanical obstruction.
    • Small-bowel series with barium sulfate can confirm diagnosis.
  • Complications
    • Bowel dilation → increased mural tension → decreased mucosal perfusion → bacterial proliferation → higher risk of necrosis & perforation.
    • Mortality:
    • ~10% with small-bowel dilation.
    • ~30% with necrosis & perforation.
  • Management
    • Initial conservative approach: Nasogastric suction to decompress bowel.
    • Surgical intervention (laparotomy) if obstruction does not resolve spontaneously.
  • Bowel Intussusception:
  • Rare cause of early postoperative obstruction in adults but accounts for 10% of cases in children.
  • ~90% occur within the first 2 postoperative weeks, with >50% occurring in the first week.
  • Most common after retroperitoneal & pelvic surgeries.
  • Types & Characteristics
    • Unlike idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, postoperative cases are usually ileoileal or jejunojejunal.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Vomiting, abdominal distension, pain after laparotomy in children.
  • Complications & Management
    • Early surgical intervention prevents perforation & peritonitis.
    • Definitive treatment: Operative intervention.
    • If the bowel is viable, a simple reduction of intussusception is sufficient.
  • Post-operative constipation and fecal impaction:
Postoperative Constipation
  • Common after surgery, primarily due to opioid use for pain control.
  • Risk factors:
  • Predisposing conditions (e.g., megacolon, paraplegia).
  • Advanced age.
  • Use of anticholinergic & narcotic medications.
  • Symptoms:
  • Early: Anorexia, obstipation, or paradoxical diarrhea.
  • Advanced cases: Severe distension, risk of colonic perforation.
  • Diagnosis: Rectal examination.
  • Management:
  • Manual removal of fecal impaction.
  • Enemas with repeat digital examinations.
Barium Impaction
  • Occurs when barium from preoperative imaging hardens in the colon, typically affecting the right colon (site of water absorption).
  • More difficult to manage than fecal impaction.
  • Symptoms: Like bowel obstruction.
  • Treatment:
    • Enemas.
    • Polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solutions
    • Diatrizoate sodium (Hypaque) enema
    • Surgery is rarely needed.
  • Abdominal Compartment Syndrome:
  • Rare but life-threatening complication caused by increased intra- abdominal pressure.
  • Common in aggressively resuscitated patients (e.g., burn, trauma patients).
  • Like extremity compartment syndrome but lacks the "5 Ps" (pain, paresthesia, pallor, paralysis, pulselessness).
  • Pathophysiology
    • Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is measured by bladder pressure.
    • Pressures >30 mmHg are dangerous, leading to:
    • Reduced cardiac venous return (IVC compression) → Decreased preload & cardiac output.
    • Compromised venous outflow from the bowel & kidneys → Bowel ischemia & renal failure.
  • Diagnosis & Management
    • High index of suspicion, rapid diagnosis, and early intervention are critical.
    • Definitive treatment: Emergency abdominal decompression via laparotomy to restore organ perfusion.
  • Post-operative Pancreatitis:
  • Accounts for ~10% of all acute pancreatitis cases.
  • Higher risk in biliary tract surgery:
    • 1% after cholecystectomy.
    • 8% after common bile duct (CBD) exploration.
    • Worse prognosis in patients with preoperative biliary pancreatitis.
  • Pathogenesis
    • Mechanical trauma or pancreatic manipulation
    • Compromised blood supply to the pancreas.
  • Complications & Prognosis
    • Often necrotizing, with a higher risk of pancreatic insufficiency.
    • Postoperative pancreatitis has 3–4x higher complications than biliary or alcoholic pancreatitis.
    • Mortality rate: 30–40%.
  • Post-operative Hepatic Dysfunction:
  • Higher risk after:
    • Pancreatectomy, biliary bypass, portacaval shunt.
  • Types of Postoperative Hyperbilirubinemia
1. Pre-hepatic Jaundice (Bilirubin Overload)
  • Causes:
    • Hemolysis (e.g., incompatible transfusion, ECMO, congenital hemolytic diseases like sickle cell disease).
    • Hematoma reabsorption.
    • Hepatotoxic drugs, prolonged fasting, malnutrition, anesthesia effects.

2. Hepatocellular Insufficiency (Most Common Cause)

  • Injurious factors: Drugs, hypotension, hypoxia, sepsis.
  • Benign postoperative intrahepatic cholestasis:
    • Common after hypotension & multiple transfusions.
    • Can occur in patients on total parenteral nutrition (TPN).
    • Serum bilirubin: 2–20 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase, but typically afebrile.
    • Resolves by postoperative week 3.

3. Post-hepatic Obstruction (Biliary Causes)

  • Causes:
    • Direct surgical injury to the bile ducts.
    • Retained common bile duct (CBD) stones.
    • Bile duct tumor or pancreatitis.
    • Acute postoperative cholecystitis (1/3 of cases involve jaundice even without clear obstruction).
  • Diagnosis
    • Liver function tests (LFTs) are not specific for the cause or severity.
    • Key diagnostic tests:
    • Liver biopsy, ultrasound, and CT scan.
    • Transhepatic or endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERCP).
  • Management
    • Monitor renal function closely (risk of renal failure)
    • Treat the underlying cause if identified
    • Supportive/expectant management for benign cases.
  • Post-operative Cholecystitis:
  • Differences from Common Acute Cholecystitis
    • Frequently acalculous (70–80%).
    • More common in males (75%).
    • Progresses rapidly to gallbladder necrosis.
    • Poor response to conservative therapy.
  • Pathogenesis
    • Chemical or ischemic injury in some cases.
    • Unclear causes in others, but potential contributing factors include:
    • Biliary stasis & sludge formation.
    • Biliary infection.
    • Gallbladder ischemia.
  • Management
    • Urgent recognition & intervention due to risk of rapid progression to necrosis.
    • Conservative treatment is often ineffective → Cholecystectomy is usually required.
Genitourinary complications:
  • Peri-operative Kidney Injury:
  • Rapid decline in renal function occurring over hours to days.
  • ACS-NSQIP Definition: Serum creatinine increase >2 mg/dL.
  • Causes & Risk Factors
    • Ischemia (shock, hypoperfusion).
    • Sepsis.
    • Hypovolemia & bleeding.
    • Nephrotoxins (e.g., contrast dye, aminoglycosides, NSAIDs).
    • Cardiovascular failure.
  • Types of Postoperative AKI
  • 1. Prerenal AKI (Most Common Postoperative Form)
    • Caused by poor renal perfusion (e.g., hypovolemia, renal artery obstruction, heart failure).
    • Treatment:
    • Aggressive fluid resuscitation to restore perfusion.
    • Optimize cardiac output.
  • 2. Intrinsic AKI (Acute Tubular Necrosis – ATN)
    • Caused by prolonged/severe ischemia → Tubular epithelial necrosis, sloughing, and cast formation.
    • Treatment:
    • Avoid nephrotoxic agents.
    • Supportive care (fluids, electrolyte management).
    • Recovery takes time.
  • 3. Postrenal AKI (Obstruction)
    • Most commonly due to urinary retention (to be discussed separately).
    • Treatment:
    • Relieve obstruction (e.g., catheterization, surgical intervention if needed).
  • Prevention
    • Early identification of high-risk patients.
    • Avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
    • Maintain hemodynamic stability (adequate perfusion & oxygenation).
  • Post-operative urinary retention:
  • Causes:
    • Neural disruption of bladder emptying.
    • Bladder overdistension (>500 mL inhibits contraction).
  • Risk Factors
    • Prolonged surgery (>3 hours).
    • Large volumes of IV fluids.
    • Sacral plexus trauma (e.g., during abdominoperineal resection) → Requires indwelling catheter for 4–5 days.
    • Inguinal hernia patients with preexisting prostatic hypertrophy should have their prostate treated before surgery.
  • Prevention
    • Preoperative voiding before entering the OR.
    • Indwelling Foley catheter indications:
    • Surgeries >3 hours.
    • High IV fluid administration.
    • Catheter removal if the patient can ambulate within a few hours.
  • Management
    • Acute urinary retention treatment: Bladder catheterization.
    • Catheter removal if residual urine is <1000 mL and there are no signs of prolonged retention.
Infectious complications:
  • Post-operative pneumonia:
  • The most common pulmonary complication in patients who die after surgery with a mortality rate of 20–40%.
  • Predisposing Factors
    • Atelectasis, aspiration, copious secretions.
    • Impaired bronchial clearance due to:
    • Weak postoperative cough.
    • Mucociliary transport dysfunction (from endotracheal intubation).
    • Compromised alveolar macrophage function
    • Loss of ciliary coordination & squamous metaplasia weaken antibacterial defenses.
  • Microbiology & Pathogenesis
    • >50% of postoperative pneumonias are caused by Gram- negative bacilli.
    • Polymicrobial infections are common, usually from aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions.
  • Risk factors for nosocomial pneumonia:
  • Azotemia, prolonged intubation, severe systemic infection.
  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP):
    • Most common surgical infection in ICU
    • Occurs 2-3 days after intubation
    • Pseudomonas aeruginosa & Klebsiella are common ICU pathogens.
    • Can survive in ventilator reservoirs.
    • Late VAP (> 5 days) > likely MDR bacteria
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Fever, tachypnea, increased secretions.
    • Signs of pulmonary consolidation on physical exam.
    • Chest X-ray findings: Patchy opacification or localized consolidation.
  • Prevention
    • Respiratory exercises, deep breathing, coughing to prevent atelectasis.
    • Orotracheal is better than nasotracheal intubation
    • Shorter duration
    • Adequate postoperative pain control to prevent shallow breathing.
    • Prophylactic antibiotics do NOT reduce pneumonia incidence or Gram-negative colonization.
  • Diagnosis & Management
    • Definitive diagnosis requires sputum sample from the trachea via endotracheal suctioning.
    • Treatment involves targeted antibiotic therapy
  • Urinary tract infection (UTI):
  • Most frequently acquired nosocomial infection.
  • Common contributing factors:
    • Preexisting urinary tract contamination.
    • Urinary retention.
    • Instrumentation (e.g., catheterization).
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Cystitis (lower UTI): Dysuria, mild fever.
    • Pyelonephritis (upper UTI): High fever, flank tenderness, possible sepsis.
  • Diagnosis
    • Urinalysis for initial evaluation.
    • Urine culture for confirmation.
  • Prevention
    • Short catheter duration (<48 hours)
    • Treat urinary tract contamination before surgery.
    • Prevent or promptly treat urinary retention.
    • Use careful instrumentation
  • Management
    • Adequate hydration.
    • Proper bladder drainage.
    • Targeted antibiotic therapy.
  • Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
  • Organisms:
    • Staph epidermidis and other GBC – most common
    • GNB: Less common
    • Fungal – critically ill patients
  • Treatment:
    • Catheter removal
    • Long-course antibiotics
  • Prevention:
    • Proper insertion
  • Clostridium Difficile Colitis
  • Ranges from asymptomatic colonization to severe toxic colitis.
  • Major risk factor: Perioperative antibiotic use.
  • Transmission: Likely via hospital personnel.
  • Diagnosis
    • Stool testing for C. difficile toxin (cytopathic strain identification).
    • Stool culture for organism confirmation.
    • Severe cases: Colonoscopy shows pseudomembranes.
  • Prevention
    • Strict handwashing and enteric precautions.
    • Minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use.
  • Management
    • First-line treatment: Oral vancomycin
    • Severe cases may require additional interventions (e.g., fecal microbiota transplantation in refractory cases).
  • Drug-resistant organisms
  • Common MDROs:
    • Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
    • Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE).
  • Causes & Transmission
  • Increased antibiotic usage in both inpatient & outpatient settings contributes to resistance.
  • Primary mode of transmission in institutions: Direct patient contact.
  • Prevention Strategies
    • Strict hand hygiene.
    • Barrier precautions (gloves, gowns, isolation protocols).
    • Continuous surface decontamination.
    • Discontinuation of inappropriate antibiotic use to limit colonization.
  • Post-operative fever
  • Occurs in ~40% of patients after major surgery.
  • Most cases self-resolve, but fever may indicate serious infection and requires evaluation.
  • Features Suggestive of Infection
    • Preoperative trauma.
    • ASA class >2.
    • Fever onset after the 2nd postoperative day.
    • Initial temperature >38.6°C.
    • Postoperative WBC count >10,000/μL.
    • Serum BUN ≥15 mg/dL.
    • Presence of ≥3 of these factors → Near 100% likelihood of bacterial infection.
  • Timing & Differential Diagnosis
    • Fever within the first 48 hours → Most commonly atelectasis (resolves with lung expansion).
    • Fever after the second postoperative day:
    • Catheter-related phlebitis.
    • Pneumonia.
    • Urinary tract infection (UTI).
    • Fever after postoperative day 5:
    • Wound infection.
    • Anastomotic breakdown.
    • Intra-abdominal leak or abscess.
    • Sepsis investigation required if temperature >39°C & no wound signs → Abdominal & pelvic CT scan recommended.
    • Fever beyond the first week:
    • Drug allergy.
    • Transfusion reaction.
    • Septic pelvic vein thrombosis.
    • Intra-abdominal abscess.
  • Diagnostic Approach
    • Directed history & physical examination.
    • Targeted laboratory & radiologic studies based on suspected cause.
    • Early imaging (CT abdomen/pelvis) if high fever (>39°C) without clear infection source.
Hematological complications:
  • Venous Thromboembolism
  • Pathophysiology (Virchow's Triad)
    • Hypercoagulable state.
    • Venous stasis
    • Vessel damage
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Lower extremity swelling
    • Hypoxia & pleuritic chest pain
  • Diagnosis
    • First-line: Duplex ultrasound for DVT.
    • Alternative imaging (more costly/invasive):
    • CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for PE.
    • MRI or venography for detailed vascular assessment.
  • Prevention (More Effective than Treatment)
    • Standard prophylaxis:
    • Heparin therapy (regular or low-molecular-weight heparin).
    • Sequential compression devices (SCDs).
    • Early ambulation.
    • Inferior vena cava (IVC) filters: Considered for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or progressive VTE despite adequate therapy.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
  • Postoperative thrombocytopenia: ≥50% reduction in platelet count.
  • HIT typically occurs within 1 week of heparin therapy initiation.
  • More common with unfractionated heparin than LMWH.
  • Diagnosis & Management
    • Suspected HIT:
    • Discontinue all heparin products (including flushes & heparin- coated catheters).
    • Perform HIT antibody assay (anti-PF4 assay).
    • Confirmed HIT:
    • Avoid further heparin use.
    • If anticoagulation is needed, use a direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI):
    • Lepirudin (contraindicated in renal failure).
    • Argatroban (contraindicated in hepatic failure).
    • Long-term anticoagulation transition:
    • Warfarin may be used but should NOT be initiated during the acute phase, as it increases the risk of thrombosis.
  • Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
  • Abnormal, widespread activation of the coagulation system.
  • Causes & Risk Factors
    • Sepsis.
    • Shock.
    • Trauma & burns.
    • Fat, cholesterol, or amniotic embolism.
    • Massive hemorrhage.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Petechiae & Ecchymoses.
    • Bleeding from IV lines, injection sites, surgical wounds.
    • Severe cases: Frank hemorrhage from orifices & surgical sites.
  • Diagnosis & Laboratory Findings
    • Prolonged PT & aPTT.
    • Low fibrinogen.
    • Elevated D-dimer.
    • Thrombocytopenia.
    • Decreased clotting factors (by thromboelastography - TEG).
  • Management
    • Replace deficient blood products based on lab results:
    • Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) – for clotting factor depletion.
    • Platelets – for thrombocytopenia.
    • Cryoprecipitate – for fibrinogen replacement.
  • Hemoperitoneum
  • No.1 cause of shock in the first 24 hours after abdominal surgery.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Usually evident within 24 hours postoperatively.
    • Signs of intravascular depletion (hypovolemic shock):
    • Tachycardia & hypotension.
    • Decreased urine output.
    • Peripheral vasoconstriction (cool, clammy skin).
    • Abdominal distension & increased girth.
    • Possible intra-abdominal hypertension or abdominal compartment syndrome.
  • Management
    • Immediate fluid resuscitation to expand intravascular volume.
    • If hypovolemic shock persists, return to the OR for surgical intervention:
    • Identify & control the bleeding source.
    • Evacuate intra-abdominal blood/clots.
    • Irrigate the peritoneal cavity with saline.
Other complications:
  • Lines
Peripheral Venous Complications
  • Phlebitis
    • Occurs at the peripheral IV catheter site, often after postoperative day 3.
    • Triad of symptoms: Induration, edema, and local tenderness.
    • Management:
    • Remove the catheter at the first sign of inflammation (redness, induration, or edema).
    • Usually self-resolving, no further treatment required.
  • Suppurative Phlebitis
    • Infected thrombus at the venous catheter site.
    • Most common causative organism: Staphylococcus species.
    • Signs:
    • Purulent drainage from venipuncture site.
    • High fever & positive blood cultures.
    • Management:
    • Surgical excision of the affected vein.
    • Incision extended proximally to the first open collateral.
    • Wound care with secondary healing.
Central Venous Complications
  • Mechanical Complications
    • Pneumothorax (with subclavian & internal jugular vein access).
    • Prevention: Ultrasound guidance reduces arterial injury & complications.
  • Air Embolism (Occurs During Placement or Removal)
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Air enters the venous system → Lodges in the right atrium → Prevents adequate filling → Hypotension & tachycardia.
  • Prevention:
    • Place the patient in the Trendelenburg position (head-down) during CVL insertion/removal.
    • Emergency Treatment:
    • Aspirate air with a syringe.
    • If unsuccessful, position the patient right-side up & head down to dislodge air & restore circulation.
  • Right Atrial Perforation (Rare but Can Lead to Cardiac Tamponade).
  • Arterial Injury → Risk of pseudoaneurysm, bleeding, or stroke.
    • Prevention: Use ultrasound to reduce arterial puncture risk.
  • Swan-Ganz (Flow-Directed Balloon-Tipped) Catheter Complications
    • Right atrial perforation (most common).
    • Intracardiac knotting of the catheter.
    • Cardiac dysrhythmias.
    • Pulmonary hemorrhage
  • Prevention:
    • Careful catheter advancement
    • Verify the catheter tip position before inflating the balloon.
Arterial Line Complications
  • Used for continuous blood pressure monitoring.
  • Potential complications:
    • Thrombosis → Risk of acute limb ischemia → Requires immediate revascularization.
    • Bleeding or aneurysm.
  • Prevention:
    • Before radial artery line placement, check ulnar artery patency using the Allen test.
  • Drains
  • Indications for Intraoperative Drain Placement
    • Prevents fluid accumulation after:
    • Cholecystectomy.
    • Splenectomy.
    • Colectomy.
    • Postoperatively, drains may be used for fluid collections or abscess drainage.
  • Drain Management & Risks
    • Strict documentation
    • Older Penrose drains should generally be avoided due to infection risk.
    • Large, rigid drains pose risks of:
    • Erosion into adjacent organs or vessels.
    • Fistula formation or bleeding.
    • Softer Silastic drains reduce risks and should be removed early.
  • Retained foreign bodies
  • Most retained objects: Sponges & surgical instruments.
  • Most affected body cavities:
    • Abdomen (most common).
    • Thoracic cavity (second most common).
  • Prevention
    • Improved communication within the operating room.
    • Formal sponge & instrument counts.
    • Intraoperative & postoperative radiography when needed.
